**Fix pass (2026-11-18):** the class-A items, the two coupled hardware-refusal
defects (B6, B7) and the release item D2 are closed in source, and A8 has a
documented recovery matrix. See §11 for the per-item state; every fix there is
**unverified on hardware** and is exercised only by the host simulator
(`ENVIRONMENT=HOST_SIMULATOR`, `ACTUATION_VERIFIED=0`), host contract tests and
the two CI jobs.

**One-line verdict:** the repository is a *fail-closed research harness*. Every
component that would mutate a GPU is present and internally consistent, but the
product asked about — one deployable signed image that selects cards at runtime
and unlocks several of them on arbitrary supported machines — is blocked by
three separate classes of work: **per-machine build coupling** (selection,
ESP identity, stock profile), **unproven privileged operations** (vendor Stop,
DMA quiescence, firmware acceptance), and **release engineering** (signing,
recovery, hardware-in-the-loop). The count is in the summary above: **22% of
the source obligations are met, and none of them is verified**, because the
privileged operations are the ones that need silicon.

## 0. What the source can do today

| Artifact | Built by | What it does | Mutates a GPU? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `GPU-TOPOLOGY-DIAGNOSTIC.EFI`, `MSI-B850-*.EFI`, Windows-handoff variants | `Build-Gpu-Topology-Diagnostic.ps1` | read-only inventory, ROM/fuse/GOP/policy observation | No — separate PE image, never links the unlock core |
| `GPU-ACTIVE-PREP-*.EFI`, `…-DXE-*.efi` | `Build-Experimental-MSVC.ps1`, `Build-Dxe-Driver.ps1` (default) | boots, discovers, validates cold profile, refuses before mutation (`GU_ACTIVE_SEQUENCE_PREPARE_ONLY`, `GU_PREFLIGHT_ONLY 1`) | No |
| `GPU-SEQUENCE-COMPILE-ONLY-*.EFI` | same builders, `-SyntheticCompileProfile` | compiles the ordered multi-target source; both entrypoints return `EFI_UNSUPPORTED` immediately | No |
| `GPU-{ONE-TARGET,SEQUENCE}-UNVERIFIED-ACTUATION-*.EFI` | same builders, `-AcceptUnverifiedActuation` | the real transaction, one card at a time, ordered | **Yes** — compiled in CI (§11.14) but never run; per-machine, `ACTUATION_VERIFIED=0` |
| `GPU-RUNTIME-SELECTION-{PREP,UNVERIFIED-ACTUATION}[-DXE].{EFI,efi}` | same builders, `-RuntimeSelection` | same profiles, but the target list comes from the `GuTargets` variable at boot instead of the build | only with `-AcceptUnverifiedActuation`, which still requires the waiver |

CI (`gpu-topology-diagnostic.yml`) compiles the diagnostic and the app/DXE
prepare and synthetic variants on `windows-latest`, **and since §11.14 the
admitted image too**: application and DXE, one target and an ordered pair, built
with `-RuntimeEsp` because a runner has no reviewed GUID and a waived image may
not use the synthetic one. Those builds are never uploaded, and the host job
diffs the admitted image against the checked one. What CI still cannot do is run
anything: the actuating path is compiled, not executed.

## 1. The gates, exactly as they stand

| Gate | Location | Default | With `-AcceptUnverifiedActuation` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Build admission | `port.h:130-146` (`GU_ACTUATION_ADMITTED`) | 0 | 1 |
| Write/DMA/FLR helpers | `port.h:148-157` (`GU_PREFLIGHT_ONLY`) | 1 | 0 |
| Runtime multi-target refusal | `gpu_discovery.c:977-981` | refuses `selected_count != 1` | admits ordered list |
| Single-target compile gate | `gpu_discovery.c:26-28` | `#error` unless one address | lifted |
| Vendor Stop for 0x2684 / 0x220a | `msi_release.c:1055-1060` | `EFI_UNSUPPORTED` | logged admission |
| Turing actuation | `profile.c:268-271` | `TURING_PREPARE=REFUSED` | unchanged |
| PROM authenticity | `profile.c:78-99` | structural + digest log only | unchanged |

The gates fail closed and early, log a reason, and never retry. That design is
sound and should survive every item below.

## 2. Class A — architecture coupling to the build machine (P0)

These are the items that make "dynamic hardware selection" impossible today.

### A1. Target selection is a compile-time constant — **P0**
`gpu_discovery.c:19-31` includes a generated `gpu-selection.h`;
`GU_GPU_SELECTION_COUNT`/`GU_GPU_SELECTION_LOCATIONS` are baked in by
`Gpu-Selection-Build.ps1` from `-SelectionBdf(s)`. With no requested list, only
the `count == 1` case auto-selects, and anything else selects nothing and says
why (`REASON=SELECTION_AMBIGUOUS`, `gpu_discovery.c:306-388`, §11.22). There is no
runtime inventory menu, no UEFI-variable policy, no "all supported cards"
default. A card added to a slot, or a BDF that shifts after a firmware update,
turns into `EFI_UNSUPPORTED` with no way to recover without a rebuild.
*Exit criteria:* runtime selector over the live inventory with the ordered
coordinator unchanged, plus a documented default policy and an operator override
that does not require recompilation.

**Status (2026-11-18): fixed in source — unverified on hardware.** `-RuntimeSelection`
builds carry no `gpu-selection.h`; the target list is the `GuTargets` UEFI
variable (`src/gpu_selection.c`), read once per boot, defaulting to the
single-card policy when unset and to every supported card for `ALL`. The
console path records a lone card automatically and offers a numbered choice on
a multi-card machine. See §11.1.

### A2. The Windows ESP is identified by a build-time partition GUID — **P0**
`boot_io.c:468-482` requires the ESP device path to match `WindowsPartition`;
`gpu_windows_path.c:21-40` compares the GPT GUID byte-for-byte;
`src/boot_profile.h` demands a private `local/boot_profile.h`, and
`boot_profile.example.h` says "Do not remove or widen those guards to make
another machine boot." One image therefore belongs to one Windows installation.
*Exit criteria:* runtime ESP identification (enumerate ESPs, require exactly one
with `\EFI\Microsoft\Boot\bootmgfw.efi`, cross-check the `BootOrder` entry that
names it), keeping the strict single-ESP refusal.

**Status (2026-11-18): fixed in source — unverified on hardware.** `-RuntimeEsp`
drops the compiled pin. A volume qualifies only if its device path carries
exactly one GPT partition with the EFI-system type (`GuWindowsEspPathCandidate`),
it is not USB and not this image's own volume, and it actually contains
`\EFI\Microsoft\Boot\bootmgfw.efi`; the existing "exactly one match"
refusal is unchanged, so a second ESP cannot be silently chosen. The
`BootOrder` cross-check is implemented in source (§11.25): an option that names
the selected volume is required, a readable order that names no such volume is
refused, and an order this image cannot read is logged as unchecked rather than
silently accepted. It has not been run against a real `BootOrder`.

### A3. Multi-GPU execution exists but only behind the waiver — **P0**
`gpu_discovery.c:26-28` (compile) and `:977-981` (runtime) both refuse
`N > 1` unless admitted; `unlock_execution.c:148-190` is a correct sequential
loop, but nothing has ever executed two cards. Production requires *verified*
multi-target admission, which needs C1–C4 resolved first.
*Exit criteria:* two physical cards, ordered execution, per-card completion
records, peer snapshots unchanged, handover verified.

**Status (2026-11-18): build coupling removed; hardware evidence still absent.**
A runtime-selection image cannot know the target count at build time, so the
static "exactly one address" gate no longer applies to it; the runtime
admission (`selected_count != 1` without `GU_ACTUATION_ADMITTED`) is unchanged
and still refuses multi-card actuation without the waiver. The remaining work
is the two-card harness in C1–C4/C9, not code. See §11.2.

### A4. The stock profile is a compile-time selector — **P0**
`port.h:57-72` requires exactly one of `GU_ENTRY_LATCHED_SS1_FULL`,
`…_PRESERVE`, `GU_STOCK_PROFILE_ORIGINAL_03100062`,
`OBSERVED_03000062`; the expected post-write selectors are constants
(`GU_SS0_UNLOCK 0x88888888`, `GU_SS1_UNLOCK 0x8`,
`unlock_610.c:29-31`). A second card whose cold selectors differ, or a machine
whose stock values differ from the chosen variant, cannot use the same image.
*Exit criteria:* profile detection from the latched entry values, with the
per-variant expectations and the same latching discipline
(`profile.c:307-312`).

**Status (2026-11-18): partly fixed — the build choice is now enforced.** An
image built for one captured stock value refuses a card presenting another,
before any write (§11.11). The compile-time *selection* remains compile-time:
the profile chooses between code paths guarded by
`#ifdef GU_ENTRY_LATCHED_SS1_FULL`/`_PRESERVE` across `port.c` (`:565`, `:570`,
`:761`), not just a value, and the two entry-latched policies are
indistinguishable before the write, so no probe can choose between them. Turning
that into a runtime choice is a behavioural change in the most destructive part
of the path with no cold-state evidence behind it; guessing here would be exactly
the failure mode the repository's own gates exist to prevent. See §11.11 and
§11.7.

### A5. Architecture coverage is uneven and partly absent — **P0**
* Turing is refused in prepare (`profile.c:268-271`) *and* ships no payload:
  `TU102-ASSETS/` contains only a README, while `profile.c:27-35` pins hash
  expections for five TU102 files.
* Ampere is admitted (assets pinned, `profile.c:18-26`) but the transaction
  branches it takes are the generic ones, since `is_ad102()` is
  `gpu_is_ada_device()` (`unlock_610.c:353-356`).
* All Ada IDs share the "AD102" permission/readout/WPR offsets
  (`unlock_610.c:1385-1424`, `1715`, `1793`) while AD104/AD106/AD107 SKUs are
  assumed to have identical register geometry. Nothing verifies that per SKU.
*Exit criteria:* per-SKU register tables justified by captured ROM/register
dumps, Turing either implemented with payloads and a signed-loader contract or
refused at *build* time (not only at prepare).

**Status (2026-11-18): partly fixed — the unsafe half is now refused, and
Turing is refused when the image is built.** The actuation paths refuse every Ada
id whose register geometry was never captured
(`src/gpu_sku_geometry.[ch]`), so an AD104/106/107 card can no longer be driven
with AD102 offsets; the read-only diagnostic deliberately still runs, because
capturing that geometry is the work needed to add a row. Turing is now refused at
*build* time as well as at prepare: `src/turing_assets.h` fails any build that
defines `GU_TURING_ACTUATION`, because this tree pins five TU102 hashes and
ships no payload bytes, and it pins the reviewed manifest row count so the table
cannot be trimmed while Turing stays admitted (§11.9). What remains open is the data: a captured
table per SKU, and a Turing payload plus a signed-loader contract. See §11.9.

### A6. Firmware assets must be re-read from removable media on every boot — **P0**
`GuBootOpen` refuses any image not launched from USB (`boot_io.c:168`) and
requires a writable `\AD102-UNLOCK` directory; `GuBootLoadAssets`
(`boot_io.c:370-425`) reads five files, including the 84,277,400-byte
`gsp_ga10x.bin`, from the USB root or a build-time-pinned ESP
(`ReadPinnedAssetFromConfiguredEsp`). Hash equality is checked
(`boot_io.c:403`) but no signature is. Operationally: the USB stick is part of
the runtime, not just the installer.
*Exit criteria:* an install step that places assets on the ESP with an
integrity check, or embedding, plus a defined story for the 84 MB payload.

**Status (2026-11-18): partly fixed — the install step exists.** An explicit
`GU_ASSET_INSTALL_ONLY` build verifies the pinned bundle from removable media,
copies it to the configured Windows ESP, reads every file back and re-verifies
it, and only then records the bundle in NVRAM (`asset_install.[ch]`,
`GuAssetInstallStage`). The launch rule is unchanged: the image must still be
started from USB, and the record authorizes nothing — it reports
`CURRENT`/`STALE`/`ABSENT`/`CORRUPT` at load. Signature acceptance (C3/C4/D1) is
still open, and so is the 84 MB embed-versus-stream decision. See §11.10.

### A7. Nothing persists across boots; the transaction is re-applied every boot — **P1**
`dxe_main.c:18-21`, `:112-125` registers a `ReadyToBoot` event and runs the whole
sequence each boot. There is no marker that the card was already processed, no
idempotency rule beyond the cold-state checks, and `driver_nvram.c` only
manages `Driver####`/`DriverOrder` entries. Whether the stock Windows driver
accepts a re-modified card on the Nth boot is unverified.
*Exit criteria:* a defined contract — either "always re-apply, and here is the
evidence it is safe", or a persisted state record with a documented reset path.

**Status (2026-11-18): partially fixed in source — the record exists, the
contract does not.** Both entrypoints now write a fixed-size NVRAM record in two
phases (`INTENT` before the first mutation, `OUTCOME` after) and report it at
the next boot, so an interrupted transaction is visible instead of invisible.
The record is deliberately **inert**: nothing branches on it, because whether
re-application is safe is unproven. "Always re-apply" therefore remains the
behaviour, and this item stays open until C1–C4 produce the evidence. See §11.8.

### A8. Recovery is physical only — **P1**
`unlock_610.c:846-857` retains all firmware-visible memory whenever the engine
did not stop; `app.c:198-210` and `dxe_main.c:69-80` halt or power down instead
of recovering. `GuBootOpen` disables the firmware watchdog
(`boot_io.c:214-217`), so a hung transaction has no automatic reset. There is
no rollback, no re-flash path, and no post-failure diagnostic except the USB
log.
*Exit criteria:* documented, tested recovery matrix (mid-transaction power
loss, Stop hang, FLR refusal, partial multi-GPU) with a software-visible state
that survives the failure.

**Status (2026-11-18): the mechanism and the documented matrix exist; no bound
is claimed and nothing is verified on hardware.** A per-class recovery matrix now
exists (§11.15), grounded in log lines this source prints and in the A7 record,
with the simulator row that exercises each software half.

**The mechanism.** The
software-visible state from A7 (above) now survives a failure, and a build can
now bound the firmware timer: it is armed once in `GuBootOpen` for a build that
sets `GU_WATCHDOG_SECONDS`, and cancelled before the handover, so a hang inside
the sequence resets the machine instead of freezing it with a half-written card
(§11.12). The default build arms nothing, because no worst-case duration has been
measured (C2/C6) — a timer shorter than the transaction would reset a machine
mid-write, which is strictly worse than the current hang. Recovery itself remains
physical.

All fail closed, but each one is a machine class that cannot run the product.
These are verified from source, not inferred.

| B2 | Headless mode needs a surviving non-target GOP; non-headless needs exactly one target GOP | `msi_release.c:587-597` | no iGPU + single dGPU (the common gaming build) cannot be prepared | P0 |

| ~~B4~~ | ~~Unknown PCI capability IDs refused~~ | `checks.c:87-89` (`default: return FALSE`), pinned by `tests/test_admission_gates.py` | **pinned in source, unverified on hardware** - a real card exposing any capability outside PM/MSI/MSI-X/PCIe/vendor is refused rather than guessed at; the log says `Config: cold PCI policy refused` (§11.20) | ~~P1~~ done |

## 6. Class E — evidence the product depends on and does not have

1. Stock Windows 617.42 driver accepts a modified card (E1, P0).
2. Tensor Core numerical correctness after modification (E2, P0).
3. Tensor Core throughput / rate-limiter effect (E3, P1).
4. Recovery matrix, including mid-transaction power loss (E4, P0).
5. Multi-GPU end-to-end on real hardware (E5, P0).
6. BDF stability across firmware updates and slot changes (E6, P1).
7. Driver-update coupling: assets are pinned to the 610.43.03 lineage (E7, P1).
8. AD104/AD106/AD107 and GA102 variants with non-0x2684/0x220a IDs (E8, P1).
9. Thermal/power/long-run stability (E9, P2).
10. Interaction with Secure Boot, BitLocker, anti-cheat (E10, P2).

---

## 7. Class F — what the simulator cannot answer

`docs/HOST_SIMULATOR.md` states the limits; for this inventory the relevant ones
are: one modelled card, no SMMU, no MSI-X vector allocation, no scheduled
interrupts, no real vendor Stop callback, no power/thermal model, no Windows.
The simulator's four scenarios (`verify`) therefore constrain *ordering and
cleanup in our own code*, not any of C1–C10.

---

## 8. Ordered plan to close the inventory

| Stage | Work | Exit criteria |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **S1 — make one machine repeatable** (weeks) | A2 runtime ESP identification (done, §11.6); A6 asset install (done, §11.10); D1 signing (open); D2 CI build of the waiver path (**done, §11.14**: diffed on the host, compiled by MSVC, never published) | one image booted twice on the same machine, both boots verified from the USB log; CI builds and diffs the admitted image |
| **S2 — make selection dynamic** (weeks) | A1 runtime selector + policy; A4 profile detection; B3/B6 relaxation with evidence (MSI state handling, ReBAR/BAR>4 GiB) | one image, two different machines with different BDFs and different stock profiles, each completes without a rebuild |
| **S3 — prove the privileged path** (the long pole) | C1 bounded Stop or a replacement detach; C2 DMA quiescence proof; C3/C4 authenticated firmware acceptance | a written harness that shows the Stop callback returns within a bound, DMA is provably idle, and firmware acceptance is decided by signature, not hash |
| **S4 — multi-GPU** (after S3) | A3 verified multi-target admission; C9 interference testing; memory budget (B10) | two cards, ordered, peers unchanged, handover verified, no retained buffers |
| **S5 — recovery and coverage** (parallel from S1) | A8 recovery matrix (**documented and pinned, §11.15**); C6 timeout policy; A5 SKU coverage; E1–E5 campaign | documented recovery for each failure class; per-SKU evidence; Windows-side acceptance measured |

S3 is the item that cannot be shortened by more code review: it needs hardware
and vendor-behaviour evidence. S1 and S2 are ordinary engineering and are the
only blockers that are fully solvable in this repository.

---

## 9. What is already sound (do not redo)

* Fail-closed, logged, no-retry gate structure (`port.h`, `gpu_discovery.c`).
* Ownership records: per-platform release state, asset tables, CPU-pool
  ownership, uncertain-release retention (`port.c`, `compat.c`).
* No PROM writes anywhere; the unlock patches a RAM copy (`sim` asserts
  `PROM_WRITES=0`).
* Ordered transaction with per-step completion records and peer config
  snapshots (`gpu_execution_state.c`, `gpu_discovery.c:497-540`).
* Inventory never truncates: `GU_INVENTORY_TOO_MANY` instead of a silent cap
  (`gpu_inventory.c:63-67`).
* The simulator's ordering assertions (`SS0`, `SS1` before `FLR`, WPR2 opened
  once and closed) are the strongest evidence in the repository about our own
  sequencing.

## 11. Fix log — what actually changed (2026-11-18)

Every entry below is **fixed in source, unverified on hardware**. "Verified"
means observed in the host simulator or a host contract test with
`ENVIRONMENT=HOST_SIMULATOR`, `ACTUATION_VERIFIED=0`,
`CAN_DETACH/CAN_UNLOCK/CAN_FLASH/RECOVERY_VERIFIED=0`. No card was touched, so
no entry claims hardware behaviour.

### 11.22 C9 — two cards, modelled: an empty selection now says why, snapshots stay separate

The multi-card story was two claims with no witness: that a machine with two
NVIDIA display functions cannot have a card chosen for it, and that the
per-target config snapshot really is per target. The simulator models one card,
and the two-card expectations lived only inside the CI workflow's direct
compilation of `tests/test_gpu_discovery.c`.

`tests/test_two_card_contract.py` now runs that contract from the host suite, in
three `gpu-selection.h` configurations: preparation-only with **two** selected
locations (prepares the inventory, revalidates the unselected peer, calls
`GuInit` never), ordered single-target compilation with three declared
locations, and single-target with three locations **failing to compile** because
that build may name only one card.

`tests/test_multi_target.py` adds the model the machine cannot supply yet:
`SelectPreparedRecords` extracted from `src/gpu_discovery.c`, the real
`GuFindGpuRecordSequence` (compiled from `src/gpu_inventory.c`) and the real
`GuCheckConfig`/`GuCheckConfigPolicy` from `src/checks.c`, driven with two cards
and two independent 256-byte snapshots. 56 assertions.

| Situation | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| one card, no selection | prepared, `SELECTED=1` (unchanged) |
| two cards, no selection | nothing selected, plus the new line `ACTIVE_PREPARE=NO_SELECTION REASON=SELECTION_AMBIGUOUS NVIDIA_COUNT=2 SELECTED=0`; the entrypoint then refuses with `REASON=NO_SELECTED_TARGET` |
| no NVIDIA card at all | empty selection, `REASON=NO_NVIDIA_CARD` |
| two cards, one named | exactly that one is prepared |
| two cards, both named | both, in enumeration order - the list the waiver admits, still one at a time in the coordinator |
| a named location that is absent / duplicated | `SELECTION_CODE=5` / `=4`, unchanged |
| more locations than cards | `REASON=REQUESTED_EXCEEDS_INVENTORY` |
| a named card this image was not built for | selected by location, named as `ACTIVE_PREPARE=SELECTED_UNSUPPORTED_CARD BDF=… ID=…`; the entrypoint refuses it |

All of that is logging. `SelectPreparedRecords` answers "which records were
named", so it keeps returning success with an empty selection - a contract
`tests/test_gpu_discovery.c` pins (a two-card machine with no request yields
`inventory.count==2 && selected_count==0`), and one a read-only inventory caller
depends on. Before this entry the only trace of that state was
`ACTIVE_PREPARE=COMPLETE SELECTED=0`, with the refusal happening afterwards and
silently; now both halves say what they are.

The snapshot half is asserted directly: two snapshots with different capability
offsets report different `GU_CAPS`, admitting the second changes neither the
first card's bytes nor its verdict, a card made inadmissible by a version bump
leaves the other one admissible, and the policy never writes a snapshot. The
entrypoint's two-card guards (`REASON=MULTI_NVIDIA_GLOBAL_STATE`,
`REASON=MULTI_TARGET_WITHOUT_WAIVER`, the single-target `#error` on
`GU_GPU_SELECTION_COUNT != 1`) are pinned as source text in the same test, and
the harness's copy of `GU_GPU_PREPARED_VIEW` is compared field for field with the
real declaration so the model cannot diverge.

What this does not do: it does not put two cards in a machine. `C9` stays
partial and `B10` untouched - the per-card memory footprint (~165 MB: DMA
window, 1 MiB ROM buffer, ~80 MB radix table) is still arithmetic in the source
and unmeasured for two cards, and no byte of evidence here comes from silicon.
`M4_ONE_CARD_ONLY` therefore still applies to every donor run.

### 11.32 C5 — a read-only probe of the write set, before the first actuation

Every image in this tree that can write to a GPU has been handed to an operator
with the same implicit promise: the BAR0 offsets in it are the ones the
transaction means to touch. Nothing checked that. A wrong offset would have been
discovered by a write - on the card, once, on the day of the first actuation -
which is the worst possible time to learn it.

The write set is small and fixed. `src/vendor/unlock_610.c` reaches BAR0 through
exactly one primitive, `GuWrite32` (via `GuCompatWrite32`, bounds-checked against
`owner->bar_base`), and that primitive has one in-tree caller: `write_bar()`.
Twenty-four `write_bar()` call sites resolve to **twenty engine deltas**, applied
at both engine bases (`gu_sec2` at `0x00840000`, `gu_gsp` at `0x00110000`), plus
the two speed selectors (`0x0082381c`, `0x00823820`) that
`write_selector()` writes when the AD104 policy allows it. Forty-two words.

There is now a read-only image that reads those forty-two words, and nothing
else:

* `src/vram_blocks.h` names each word once, with the writer's own expression in
  the comment above it. It is a table of constants and cannot grow a write path.
* `ReportVramBlocks` in `src/gpu_topology_efi.c` walks that table per
  identity-verified card - the same `pci->Mem.Read` idiom, BDF check and driver
  binding check as the MSI fuse probes - and prints one line per word:
  `BLOCK=… BAR0_OFFSET=… ROLE=WRITE STATUS=OBSERVED RAW=…`, `ACCEPTANCE=UNVERIFIED`
  on every one. Two more lines report the words the writer *reads* to choose its
  writes (`GU_FEAT_PLM_OFFSET`, `GU_FEAT_READOUT_1_OFFSET`) as `ROLE=READ_CONTEXT`.
* A per-card SHA-256 over the forty-two values in table order makes the
  before/after comparison a one-line diff. The line says what it is:
  `DIGEST_CV=CHANGE_DETECTOR_ONLY`. A failed read withholds the digest and prints
  `INCOMPLETE_READ_SET=1` instead of hashing a hole.
* Opt-in only: `-VramBlockProbe` in `src/Build-Gpu-Topology-Diagnostic.ps1`,
  its own image `VRAM-BLOCK-PROBE-DIAGNOSTIC.EFI`, refused in the same build as
  an MSI source diagnostic or a GPU selection (two `#error`s and a PowerShell
  throw), and it requires `-SaveLog` so the evidence outlives the boot. Normal
  topology and active builds never compile it.

The coupling is the point, and it is machine-checked rather than reviewed.
`tests/test_vram_block_probe.py` parses `unlock_610.c`: it resolves
`eng->base`/`eng->falcon2`/`eng->fbif` against both engine initializers, the
`base + …` DMA deltas against a `falcon_dma(work, eng->base, …)` call, the
explicit `SEC2_BASE + 0x3c0` sites and every `write_selector(…)` call, then
asserts set *equality* with the header. A new `write_bar()` without a probe row
fails the suite; a probe row without a writer site fails it too. Three injected
faults were checked by hand - a dropped probe row, an added writer site at an
offset the probe does not read, and a `GuWrite32` call inside the probe body -
and each one fails.

Scoring is a gate, not a paragraph: `R4_WRITE_SET_READ_BEFORE_ACTUATION` requires
the `BEGIN` line, at least forty-two observed write-set lines
(`min_total 42`), and the `END` line's arithmetic; it forbids
`STATUS=UNAVAILABLE` on any write-set word and `INCOMPLETE_READ_SET=1`. The gate
is declared `only_if` the probe's own opening line, so a read-only boot that ran
a different image reports `RESULT=NOT_APPLICABLE` - never `PASS`.
`tests/fixtures/hardware_session/readonly_vram_blocks.txt` is a synthetic
two-card probe log; it passes all four read-only gates under `--self-test`, and
dropping a block line or marking one unreadable fails `R4` in the tests.

What it is not. The probe authenticates nothing: it reports raw words, infers no
signature slot, and prints `SECURITY_ACCEPTANCE=UNVERIFIED` on its closing line.
It does not read back a write it never issued, so there is no read-modify-write
verification loop to mistake for confirmation. It proves that a read-only image
addresses the same words `unlock_610.c` writes - a statement about two lists
agreeing, checked in the test suite, not about silicon.

What has been measured, and what has not. Measured: nothing new on hardware. This
section adds an instrument; it has not been run on the bench, and the post-state
half of the comparison needs an actuation to have completed first. Not measured,
and next: `-Only diag-vram-blocks -StageDrive G`, then the same image again after
the first actuation, with the two `WRITE_SET_SHA256` lines compared by hand.

What this does not do: no inventory row moves. `C5` stays `none`, because a
readable address before the write says nothing about what the write achieves and
the post-state half is still unmeasured; `C3` stays `none`, because a digest over
register values is not firmware acceptance. `hardware_verified` stays `false` for
all 43, and the readiness counts stay at 11 met / 15 partial / 17 not started.

### 11.31 C9/B10 — the session is an ordered list, and the workbench said "one card"

This fork is the multi-GPU architecture; single-GPU unlock already works in the
parent repository. The donor bench therefore has two cards on purpose - an RTX
4090 at `01:00.0` and an RTX 3080 at `04:00.0` - and the second card stays for
every run. The workbench did not model that. `M4_ONE_CARD_ONLY` was inherited
from the parent's single-card protocol, and `tools/donor_gate.py` refused any
stage that named more than one target, so the tool answered
`IDENTITY_NOT_SINGLE` to the machine it was built for.

What the source actually implements, in its own words (`src/port.h`): the
ordered selected-target mode means "one card is active at a time, and the
ordered list may name several targets that are executed sequentially", with each
step gated on its predecessor's completion record. Two admission switches exist
and are easy to confuse:

* **preparing** an ordered list needs no waiver. `GuDiscoverSingleGpu` returns
  before the `MULTI_TARGET_WITHOUT_WAIVER` check in a
  `GU_ACTIVE_SEQUENCE_PREPARE_ONLY` build, so `-SelectionBdfs 'a,b'` prepares two
  cards' contexts in one boot and still refuses execution;
* **executing** more than one target requires `GU_ACTUATION_ADMITTED`, which is
  the `-AcceptUnverifiedActuation` waiver (or the hosted simulator). Without it
  the image prints `REASON=MULTI_TARGET_WITHOUT_WAIVER` and stops.

The workbench now says that instead of contradicting it:

* `M4_ONE_CARD_ONLY` is `M4_DONOR_CARDS_RECORDED`: record every card by serial
  and slot, and write down the ordered BDF list before building the image. The
  card *count* is not the risk this fork carries; an unrecorded list is.
* `tools/donor_gate.py` treats identity as an **ordered list** decided by the
  preparation stage (the stage whose list the waiver will execute), not as "one
  BDF per stage". A read-only selection is an observation set - it may name more
  cards than the session will touch, and that is reported as `NOTE PEERS=` rather
  than refused. New refusals: `IDENTITY_TARGET_ORDER_CHANGED` (two boots that
  name different lists, or a reordered list), `IDENTITY_DUPLICATE_TARGET` (one
  boot naming the same card twice - the builder refuses it too, in
  `Gpu-Selection-Build.ps1`), `IDENTITY_TARGET_UNNAMED` (a multi-card machine
  where no stage named a target, so the tool would have to guess), and
  `ACTUATION_SELECTION_CHANGED` (a waiver that admits fewer targets than were
  prepared). A two-target session now composes: `DONOR_GATE VERDICT=GO
  ... TARGETS=2` on the fixtures, pinned by
  `tests/test_donor_gate.py::test_two_cards_prepared_in_one_session_reach_go`.

What has been measured, and what has not. Measured: the read-only stage observes
both cards and can be asked to walk both in order (`-0002`); the preparation
stage prepares one card per boot and refuses, twice, once per card
(`physical-prepare-0001/0002`). Not measured, and next on the list: **one boot
that prepares both cards** - `prep-selected -SelectionBdfs
'0000:01:00.0,0000:04:00.0'`, which should log two `ACTIVE_PREPARED_STEP[n]`
lines, two `ACTIVE_CONTEXT[n]=PREPARED` lines and `SELECTED=2`,
`MUTATION_AUTHORIZED=0`. `PreparePlatformContexts` allocates one platform context
per selected card and refuses an alias to the active context or a duplicate
pointer, so that log would be the first evidence that two distinct per-card
contexts coexisted in a read-only build. Never measured: any multi-target
*write*. The waived sequence image (`actuate-sequence`) exists as a variant and
has never run; a peer card's behaviour during a mutation of the other card is
therefore an untested property of this design, not a verified one.

What this does not do: no inventory row moves. `C9` (multi-GPU) and `B10`
(two-card footprint) stay where they were, `hardware_verified` stays `false` for
all 43, and the ordered-list reasoning above is code reading plus two single-card
preparation logs - not a two-card preparation, and not an actuation.

### 11.30 D5 — seven more physical runs, and the second gate no image can print

The next batch of runs on the same bench produced seven real logs: five
read-only (`diag-topology-log`, `diag-selection` with two BDFs, `diag-msi-rom`,
`diag-msi-fuse`, `diag-msi-sec2`) and two preparation-only (`prep-selected` for
`01:00.0` and for `04:00.0`). The read-only five scored `PASS` immediately. Both
preparation runs scored `FAIL FIRST_FAILED=P1_PREPARATION_REFUSED_BEFORE_MUTATION`.

P1 required `ACTIVE_APP=PREPARATION_ONLY ACTIVE_EXECUTION=REFUSED BEFORE_MUTATION=1`.
That literal is in `src/app.c`, and the grounding test could see it, so the
suite was satisfied. It is printed *after* `GuDiscoverSingleGpu` returns
success - and the preparation image is refused *by* that call
(`REASON=SELECTION_PREPARATION_ONLY`, `src/gpu_discovery.c`), so the app takes
`goto failed` and the banner never runs. `src/dxe_main.c` has the identical
shape. No preparation image can print either banner. This is the third instance
of one defect class: R2 required the strict collector's fallback (§11.29), the
donor gate let one stage's device id vouch for another (§11.29), and P1 required
an entrypoint banner that sits behind the refusal. In each case the token was a
real format string in the file it named; only reachability was wrong.

P1 now requires two lines the image does print: the refusal itself
(`ACTIVE_EXECUTION=REFUSED REASON=SELECTION_PREPARATION_ONLY BEFORE_GU_INIT=1`,
printed before any GU init) and
`ACTIVE_PREPARE=COMPLETE SELECTED=%zu NVIDIA_COUNT=%zu MUTATION_AUTHORIZED=0`.
The `dxe-prep-selected` evidence entry in the guide quoted the app's banner and
claimed the DXE entrypoint "reaches the same refusal line"; it does not, and it
now quotes the shared discovery refusal instead.

The durable defence is the same one §11.29 chose, extended: every physical log
is kept. `tests/data/hardware_session/` now holds eight captures
(`physical-readonly-0000..0005`, `physical-prepare-0001/0002`), digest-pinned in
`docs/hardware_session.json` and re-scored by `tests/test_hardware_session.py` on
every run, which also checks that every gate of the scored stage still matches
the real log. A gate that no real image can print now fails the suite. That test
is what caught P1 - not a reading of the source.

`tools/donor_gate.py` needed the other half of the same lesson. It demanded "the
same single BDF" in every stage, which a two-card bench can never satisfy: the
read-only diagnostic reports the whole machine (`GPU[0]`, `GPU[1]`, both driver
owners), and `-0001` duly named `01:00.0` and `04:00.0`, so the gate answered
`BLOCKED=IDENTITY_NOT_SINGLE` for a session that had done nothing wrong. A
census is not a choice. The gate now reads the lines where a stage says what it
actually selected (`ACTIVE_PREPARED_STEP[n]`, `SELECTION_REQUEST[n]`,
`SELECTION_STEP[n]=BEGIN`, `PASSIVE_SELECTION=`), requires a preparation or
actuation stage to select exactly one target, requires that target to be one the
read-only stage enumerated (`IDENTITY_NOT_OBSERVED` otherwise), and compares the
PCI id printed beside *that* BDF rather than the ids of every card in the
machine. An ordered multi-target read-only selection is a census; a peer card is
reported as `NOTE PEERS=1 OBSERVED=2 TARGET=01:00.0`, not refused. With those
rules the first two physical batches compose into
`DONOR_GATE VERDICT=GO SYNTHETIC=0 HARDWARE_VERIFIED=0` - the first GO this tool
has produced from real logs, and it took two wrong rules to get there.

Four findings on the machine are worth keeping, none of them a verification:

* the two boots `0000` and `0001` are identical line for line except firmware
  pointer values and the relocated whole-image digests. `MAPPED_TEXT_SHA256` is
  stable across boots (`77632902...`, `615b37a7...`); `MAPPED_IMAGE_SHA256` is
  not (`a513a554...` then `42adb7a8...` for the same driver), which is exactly
  what `RELOCATED_POSSIBLE=1` warns about. Nothing may pin a driver by the
  whole-image digest;
* `MSI_B850_VARIABLE NAME=ROM_CMN` is real (327 bytes, `ATTRS=0x7`), `CSM_CMN`
  is five bytes - too small to hold the policy table the desk research assumed -
  the BDS structure `LOCATE_STATUS=0 PRESENT=1` but `STATE=SKIPPED
  ORIGINAL_BDS_MISMATCH=1 MATCHES=0`, and the private-interface probe found no
  method to call (`CALLS=ZERO`, `NO_PRIVATE_METHOD=1`). The ROM dispatch path is
  still `ORIGINAL_ROM_DISPATCH_UNVERIFIED=1`;
* the two cards do not share a fuse state: the 4090 reads `RAW=0x1
  FUSE_VERSION=1 CANDIDATE_SLOT=1`, the 3080 `RAW=0x3 FUSE_VERSION=2
  CANDIDATE_SLOT=2`, and the SEC2 version register agrees with the SEC2 fuse per
  card (`0x1` and `0x3`). A rule calibrated on one card cannot be asserted for
  the other, and every line still carries `ACCEPTANCE=UNVERIFIED` because
  `WINDOWS_61742_DESCRIPTOR` is unknown;
* both NVIDIA drivers were loaded from one parent image
  (`PARENT_TEXT_SHA256=02a92fd4...` on both cards).

What the batch does not do: it does not mutate anything. The preparation logs end
`ACTIVE_EXECUTION=REFUSED ... BEFORE_GU_INIT=1 CAN_DETACH=0 CAN_UNLOCK=0
CAN_FLR=0` and `STOP: stage=discover status=0x8000000000000003 mutated=0
retained=0 fault=0`; the MSI probes end `NO_GPU_WRITES=1` and `CALLS=ZERO`. No
signature is authenticated, no inventory row moves, and `hardware_verified` stays
`false` for all 43. `M4_ONE_CARD_ONLY` was still in force when this batch ran; §11.31 replaces it
with `M4_DONOR_CARDS_RECORDED`, because the session this fork is for is an
ordered list over both cards rather than one card alone.

### 11.29 D5 — the first physical run failed a gate that no healthy machine can print

The first run of a signed `diag-topology-log` image on the donor bench produced
`GPU-TOPOLOGY-DIAGNOSTIC-0000.TXT` and the verifier scored it `FAIL
FIRST_FAILED=R2_ENUMERATION_COMPLETED`: the log did not contain
`PCI_OBSERVATION_ONLY=1 NOT_TOPOLOGY=1 CAN_DETACH=0 CAN_UNLOCK=0`.

The run was fine. The gate was wrong. That line is printed by
`ReportPciEvidence`, which `GuTopoDiagnosticMain` calls as
`if(!pci_ok)ReportPciEvidence(bs);` - it is the **fallback** path, taken only
when the strict collector has already failed. R2 therefore required evidence
that exists only when enumeration is broken, which no working machine can
produce; and a machine that did produce it would also print
`PCI_ENUM_FAILURE`, which R2 forbids. The grounding test could not see this: the
token is a real format string in the file it named. Only reachability was wrong,
and only silicon reports that.

R2 now requires three literal lines that a healthy run prints for different
reasons: the strict walk's own scope line
(`PCI_TOPOLOGY_SCOPE=...`), the NVIDIA owner inventory, which runs only on the
strict collector's success branch, and the report's last line
(`DIAGNOSTIC FINISHED; GPU hardware untouched.`), which a hang or an aborted save
removes. It forbids any `PCI_ENUM_FAILURE STAGE=` and
`NVIDIA_GOP_GRAPH=UNAVAILABLE GOP_CAPTURE_FAILED=1`. The fallback observation is
now an advisory (`SUPPLEMENTARY_PCI_OBSERVATION`): a healthy log does not carry
it, so its presence is a finding to explain rather than a pass to score.

The log itself is kept as a fixture of the real thing:
`tests/data/hardware_session/physical-readonly-0000.txt`, digest-pinned in
`docs/hardware_session.json` and re-scored by `tests/test_hardware_session.py` on
every run. The suite now checks every gate in the scored stage against that
physical capture - `requires` must match, `requires_any` must match one,
`forbids` must not - so a gate that no healthy run can satisfy fails the suite
instead of the operator. Reinstating the old requirement fails four tests.

The run also exposed a second, quieter gap in `tools/donor_gate.py`. Its own
printed rule said a stage that names no PCI id is refused rather than assumed,
but the check was session-wide: as long as one stage named a device id, another
stage could name a BDF and no id and still reach `VERDICT=GO`. The fixtures were
minimal enough to hide it, and the diagnostic's healthy log - which names both -
made the difference visible. Every scored stage must now name its own device id;
a stage that names a BDF but no id prints `BLOCKED IDENTITY_UNKNOWN STAGE=<stage>
reason=this_stage_named_no_pci_id`, and the actuation fixtures carry the
discovery line a real run prints.

What the run put on paper, none of it a verification: two NVIDIA cards
(`01:00.0` `10de:2684` `1043:88e6` and `04:00.0` `10de:220a` `19da:b612`), an
AMD-only console (`TOPOLOGY_VERDICT=INCOMPLETE NVIDIA_CONOUT_BLOCKER=0`,
`ERROR_CONSOLE_ISOLATION=INDEPENDENT_OBSERVED`), `GOP_COUNT=0` on both cards with
one independent iGPU GOP, both NVIDIA driver text digests identical to their
previously pinned captures (`77632902...` and `615b37a7...`), and a complete
151-line log with no dropped lines.

What it does not do: no inventory row moves and `hardware_verified` stays `false`
for all 43. Nothing was stopped, unlocked or flashed, no signature is
authenticated, and the Windows 617.42 Booter provenance is as absent as it was
before. The run is one observation of one image on one machine, recorded as such.

### 11.28 D5 — the read-only session now has a script to follow, and every line of it is checked

`docs/DONOR_HARDWARE_SESSION.md` described the gates a log has to pass, but not
the order of operations that produces the log: which image to build for which
question, what to type, and what in the resulting file answers what. An operator
with a card on the bench had the verdict tool and no runbook.

The document now carries a step-by-step guide, rendered (like the rest of it)
from `docs/hardware_session.json`: six steps from `.\src\Build-Sign-Deploy-UniversalGPU.ps1 -List`
through the build-sign-stage command, `tools/session_preflight.py`, one boot,
capture, and `tools/verify_run_log.py`; then a row for every image in
`docs/image_variants.json` whose safety class writes nothing to the GPU -
`diag-topology-log`, the three MSI B850 probes and their handoff variants,
`diag-selection`, `diag-topology-handoff`, `prep-selected` and
`dxe-prep-selected` - with the log line each one puts on paper and the inventory
item that line is waiting for. There is no script called `build-sign-stage` in
this tree, and the guide says so: `-Only <id> -StageDrive <letter>` is the
build, sign and stage step.

Two things keep it from being prose. First, the guide is data: every candidate
id, builder switch, `-StageDrive`/`-SignOnly` choice and manual-gate reference is
resolved against `docs/image_variants.json` and `src/`, and every quoted log line
is required to appear in the file named beside it with at least 12 literal
characters, so a renamed format string fails the suite instead of leaving an
instruction that does nothing. Second, the guide carries its own ceiling: a table
of what the read-only stage cannot advance - `C8` is not moved by any of it
(the `PCI_LINK=` line is printed only by the waived admission path), `C1`/`C2`/
`C5`/`C6`/`C7`/`C10` need the waived stage, and `B10`/`C9`/`E1`-`E5` need two
cards and an actuation.

What this does not do: it does not run anything. `D5` stays **partial** - the
loop is now documented and checked, and it is still a human pressing keys on a
bench. No row in `docs/readiness_status.json` moves, `hardware_verified` is
`false` for all 43 items, and the guide's own first paragraph says that no log it
describes exists.

### 11.27 D3 — every payload now says where it came from, and nothing claims more

`tools/verify_reference_assets.py` proves the bytes on this disk are the pinned
bytes. It cannot answer where they came from: the 84 MB GSP payload and the four
AD102 companions carried a local hash and nothing else.

`docs/asset_provenance.json` records, for every payload the firmware can load, a
role, the lineage (`NVIDIA 610.43.03`), the external reference the pin was taken
from (`Windows-GPU-UNLOCK/research/firmware/ada_610/artifacts-610.43.03.json`,
which is not part of this repository), and the same digest and length the
firmware enforces. `tools/verify_provenance.py` reads the asset tables out of
`src/profile.c` - not a hand-copied list - and refuses when:

* a row the image can load has no record,
* a record's digest or length disagrees with the firmware's pin,
* a record describes an asset the firmware does not load,
* a payload present on disk no longer matches its record, or
* a record claims a signature check this tree cannot perform.

The last one is a guarantee, not a comment: `signature_authenticated` must be
`false`, and the tool prints `SIGNATURE_AUTHENTICATED=0 AUTHENTICITY_UNVERIFIED=1`
on every successful run. Provenance here means named and machine-checked, never
proven genuine.

The gate also reports what it could not check: `PRESENT=10 ABSENT=5`, because the
five TU102 rows are pinned by the parent tree and this fork carries no Turing
payload bytes - `TU102-ASSETS/` is a README - which is the same reason the Turing
actuation build refuses to compile.

Evidence: `tests/test_provenance_records.py` runs the gate on the repository and
then breaks it six ways - a dropped record, a changed digest, a changed length, an
orphan record, a claimed signature, an unknown schema - and finally edits a
payload in a scratch copy and requires the gate to catch it. CI runs both the
tool and the module.

What this still does not do: it does not verify an NVIDIA signature, so a
payload that came from somewhere else and was pinned after the fact would still
pass. `D3` is **partial**: provenance is recorded, enforced and honest about its
own limit; authenticity needs a signature chain this tree does not have.

### 11.26 C10 — the resume script now says what it is, and what it cannot be

Resume is the one part of this transaction that runs when no code of ours does.
`GuRegisterS3` installs two boot-script writes - `SS0` at `BAR+0x82381c`,
`SS1` at `BAR+0x823820`, each a single 32-bit write - and firmware executes them
on wake. Everything after that is Windows' driver.

That was described as "no resume verification" in prose and nowhere else. The
log now carries the claim it can actually support:

```
S3_RESUME=UNVERIFIED WHY=NO_RESUME_HOOK BAR_BASE_MAY_MOVE=1 ADDRESSES=2 WIDTH=UINT32
```

The second field is the hazard worth naming: a boot script writes a **physical
address**, computed from this boot's BAR base. If Windows reassigns BAR0 before
the machine sleeps, the resume writes land in unrelated MMIO - and the image has
no way to observe that it happened, because nothing of ours runs at resume and
the card is not addressable from the next boot's read-only path. Arming the
script is therefore a statement about what was registered, not about what will
be true when the machine wakes.

Evidence: `tests/test_unlock_execution_contract.py` already compiled the real
`GuRegisterS3` against a modelled `EFI_S3_SAVE_STATE_PROTOCOL` and pinned the two
addresses, both values, the single 32-bit width, one attempt per card, a failure
on either write retaining the platform, a lost platform between writes, and the
refusals before any firmware call (no BAR, BAR too small or wrapping, unsafe
state, no protocol, no `Write`). It now captures the log and pins the new line,
so a future change cannot quietly drop the admission or upgrade it into a claim
of a verified resume.

What this still does not do: it cannot verify a resume, because nothing of ours
runs after one, and it cannot keep the addresses valid across a BAR reassignment
it does not control. `C10` is therefore **partial**: the registered action set is
pinned and its limit is named, the verification half needs a resume-time hook or
hardware evidence this tree cannot produce.

### 11.25 A2 — BootOrder now decides, and an unreadable order never counts as a pass

Runtime ESP identification dropped the compiled GUID, but the exit criteria had
a second half that was never implemented: *cross-check the `BootOrder` entry
that names the selected ESP*. Without it the image could pick a volume that
carries `\EFI\Microsoft\Boot\bootmgfw.efi` while the firmware boots from a
different one.

The cross-check is now implemented in two parts. `GuBootOptionNamesDevicePath`
(`src/gpu_windows_path.c`) parses one `EFI_LOAD_OPTION` - attributes,
`FilePathListLength`, a NUL-terminated UTF-16 description, then the path - and
compares the **device-node prefix**: the nodes before the first FilePath
(media/0x04) or end (0x7f) node. An option that appends
`\EFI\Microsoft\Boot\bootmgfw.efi` therefore names the same partition, while a
different partition, controller or segment does not.
`GuBootOrderNamesVolume` walks `BootOrder`, builds each `Boot####` name, reads
it through a caller-supplied variable reader, and answers one of three things:

| Verdict | Meaning | What the caller does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GU_ORDER_NAMES` | one named option points at this volume | `BOOTORDER=NAMES_SELECTED_ESP=1` |
| `GU_ORDER_NONE` | the order was readable and nothing points here | refuse: `BOOTORDER=NONE_NAMES_SELECTED_ESP REFUSED=1` |
| `GU_ORDER_UNREADABLE` | `BootOrder` or an option could not be read in full | `BOOTORDER=UNCHECKED STATUS=… PROCEEDING=1`, the rule before this entry |

The third row is the honest one: this image does not claim a cross-check it did
not perform. An option named but absent is skipped; an option larger than the
2 KiB bound, an odd-sized `BootOrder`, a missing `BootOrder` or no
`GetVariable` at all are `UNREADABLE`, never `NONE` and never `NAMES`. The
check only exists in the runtime branch - the pinned build still matches one
compiled GUID and never reads a variable - and it runs before the volume is
published, so a contradiction cannot leave a selected volume behind.

Evidence: `tests/test_gpu_windows_path.c` drives the real predicate and the real
walk with a fake variable store - match, no match, absent option, unreadable
option, missing `BootOrder`, oversized option, odd-sized order, malformed nodes
and null arguments - 56 checks, gcc and clang. `tests/test_runtime_esp_contract.py`
pins the wiring: the shared walk, both log lines, the refusal ordering, the
`#ifdef GU_RUNTIME_ESP` placement, and that the adapter reads no variable
without a runtime-services service. The UEFI sources compile under
`-DGU_RUNTIME_ESP` (checked by building the simulator with the define).

Coverage limit, stated plainly: nothing here has read a real `BootOrder`. The
predicate and the walk are executed on the host; the firmware calls around them
are compile-checked only, and a firmware whose boot options describe the ESP in
a form this comparison does not model - a short-form path, a `BBS` node, a
boot-manager that reaches the volume through a different controller alias -
degrade to `UNCHECKED` rather than to a wrong answer, and would then be refused
if the order were readable and simply did not match. `A2` is therefore **done in
source, unverified on hardware**, and the hardware half is unchanged.

### 11.24 C8 — the admission policy now reads the link, and names what it still cannot

Every gate in `src/checks.c` reads the capability chain: identity, class, header,
BAR descriptor, power state, MSI/MSI-X off, bus master, FLR. None of them read
the *link*. A card can pass all of that and still be attached over a link that
is not trained, that firmware left with ASPM enabled, or that has already
recorded a PCIe error - three states an unlock must not start in.

`GuCheckLinkState` (`src/checks.c`) reads them from the same 256-byte snapshot,
using the capability offset the admission policy already produced
(`GU_CAPS.pcie`) rather than searching for it again. It reports the first hazard
it finds, in this order:

| Verdict | What was read | Token in the log |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GU_LINK_ERROR_LOGGED` | Device Status `CED`/`NFER`/`FER`/`URD` (sticky, we do not clear them) | `PCIE_ERROR_LOGGED` |
| `GU_LINK_ASPM_ENABLED` | Link Control ASPM request, `L0s`/`L1` | `ASPM_ENABLED` |
| `GU_LINK_NOT_TRAINED` | Link Status bit 11 | `LINK_NOT_TRAINED` |
| `GU_LINK_DOWN` | Link Status bit 13 (DLL link active) | `LINK_DOWN` |
| `GU_LINK_UNUSABLE` | negotiated width 0, or speed 0/reserved | `LINK_UNUSABLE` |
| `GU_LINK_ABSENT` | no usable capability offset | `PCIE_CAPABILITY_ABSENT` |

A degraded link is *not* a refusal: x1 Gen1 still trains and still reports its
advertised maximum, so the adapter logs `PCI_LINK=OK WIDTH=1 MAX_WIDTH=16
SPEED=1 MAX_SPEED=4 ...` and continues. The active path logs that line for every
admitted card, and a refusal ends the path before `GuInit` with
`ACTIVE_EXECUTION=REFUSED REASON=PCIE_LINK LINK_REASON=<token> BDF=...`. Nothing
is mutated and nothing is allocated at that point, so nothing is marked
retained.

What is still unhandled, and says so on every line: AER lives in extended
capability space, which begins at `0x100` and is not part of the snapshot, so it
is reported as `AER=UNOBSERVED` instead of being assumed clear; hot-plug is
observed (`HOTPLUG=`, `SURPRISE=`) and logged but not refused; PCIe training
*recovery*, hot-plug events, Thunderbolt/USB4 tunnels and ASPM entry after
admission remain outside this image. The log carries
`UNHANDLED=HOTPLUG,AER` for exactly that reason.

Evidence: `tests/test_link_state.py` compiles the real `ConfigByte`,
`ConfigWord`, `GuCheckLinkState`, `GuLinkAccepted` and `GuLinkReason` and drives
crafted snapshots through every verdict, the ordering between them, each sticky
error bit, a degraded-but-healthy link, hot-plug bits, capability offsets that
are not `0x50`, and the rejections of an absent, unaligned, out-of-range or null
capability. It also compares the host mock's copy of `GU_LINK` with
`src/checks.h` token for token, so the mock cannot drift from the firmware type.
The shipped C mock (`tests/test_gpu_discovery.c`) gains a link-refusal switch and
one end-to-end case: with the link refused the active path returns
`EFI_UNSUPPORTED` without ever calling `GuInit`. The host simulator's modelled
card (`sim/sim_gpu.c`) now carries a real link - Gen4 x16, trained, active, ASPM
disabled - because a modelled card with zeroed link registers would have proved
only that the gate fires, not that a real card passes it.

### 11.23 C2 — the Stop now asks whether anything is still in flight, and refuses if it is

Clearing Bus Master stops *new* transactions. It says nothing about the ones
already posted, and every honest description of this firmware's Stop has carried
that caveat: no IOMMU/SMMU, no engine-queue readback, no bus trace. So the
release path claimed quiescence from a control bit, and the caveat lived in prose
where nothing could test it.

`NormalizeMasterAfterStop` (`src/msi_release.c`) now observes the one standard
signal that is actually readable: the PCIe Device Status **Transaction Pending**
bit (`+0x0A` of the capability, bit 5). It is polled at most
`GU_TX_PENDING_POLLS` (5) times, 1 ms apart, stopping as soon as it reads clear:

```
POST_STOP_QUIESCENCE=BUS_MASTER_ONLY TX_PENDING_CLEAR=1 POLLS=2 IOMMU=UNMANAGED QUEUE_READBACK=0 BUS_TRACE=0
POST_STOP_QUIESCENCE=REFUSED REASON=TX_PENDING_STUCK POLLS=5 IOMMU=UNMANAGED QUEUE_READBACK=0 BUS_TRACE=0
POST_STOP_QUIESCENCE=BUS_MASTER_ONLY TX_PENDING=UNOBSERVED POLLS=0 IOMMU=UNMANAGED QUEUE_READBACK=0 BUS_TRACE=0
```

A card whose bit never drains is refused with `EFI_NOT_READY` and its buffers
stay retained; a card with no PCIe capability keeps the previous behaviour and
says `TX_PENDING=UNOBSERVED` instead of implying it was checked. The observation
is logged on success as well, so "checked and clear" and "not checked" are
different lines.

Device Status is read-only, so its Pending bit is the one thing exempt from the
post-Stop drift rule (`ConfigStablePostStop`): every other byte of the 256-byte
snapshot must still match what preflight captured, and drift seen between
observations is `EFI_COMPROMISED_DATA` with the buffers retained. The capability
offset comes from the admission policy (`GuCheckConfigInitialMaster` →
`GU_CAPS.pcie`), not from a search at release time, and the range check keeps a
malformed result from pointing the read past the snapshot.

`tests/test_dma_quiescence.py` compiles the real `TxPending`,
`ConfigStablePostStop`, `WaitTxPendingClear` and `NormalizeMasterAfterStop` from
the source against a modelled card: clear on the first observation, draining on
the second poll (then success), stuck for all five (then refused, retained),
exactly five observations and four waits under a stuck card, no PCIe capability
(`UNOBSERVED`), no `Stall` service (single observation, still fail closed), a
failed config read during the poll, drift present before the read and drift
appearing between observations, an already-clear enable, a second call refused,
and the offset arithmetic of a capability that does not sit at `0x50`.
`tests/test_pci_master_transition.py` keeps its eleven transition cases on the
same extracted source with the observation disabled.

What this still does not do: it is not an IOMMU, it does not read an engine
queue back, and it does not trace a bus - the log says so on every line. The
five-observation bound is a **count, not a measured budget**: no card has been
observed to drain within 4 ms, and the wait is only ever as long as the bit
stays set. `C2` stays **partial**, and the hardware half is unchanged.

### 11.21 D5 — the donor session has a go/no-go gate, and still no hardware loop

`tools/verify_run_log.py` answers "did this stage's log prove what the plan says
it proves". It never answered "may the session advance", and the gap between
those two questions is where an unverified actuation actually gets run: a
read-only log that passes says nothing about whether preparation happened, and
nothing compared the card one stage saw with the card the next stage would touch.

`tools/donor_gate.py` composes the stage verdicts into one answer. It scores the
read-only and preparation stages with the same manifest and the same evaluator,
requires both to pass before an actuation stage is even considered, extracts the
BDF every stage prints (and the PCI id wherever a stage prints one) and refuses
unless exactly one card is named and it is the same card at every stage, and
requires every manual gate to be acknowledged by its exact id - an unknown id is
refused so a typo cannot stand in for `M6_STOCK_BOOT_AFTER_EVERY_RUN`.

| Refusal | What it catches |
| --- | --- |
| `GATE_<stage>` | a stage whose own gates failed; the failing ids are named |
| `PRIOR_STAGE_MISSING` | scoring actuation with no preparation (or preparation with no read-only contact) |
| `IDENTITY_NOT_NAMED` / `IDENTITY_NOT_SINGLE` | a stage with no BDF, or with two - the second card that `M4` forbids |
| `IDENTITY_CHANGED` / `PCI_ID_CHANGED` | a different card, or a renumbered one, between stages |
| `IDENTITY_UNKNOWN` | no stage named a PCI id at all, so nothing ties the run to a piece of silicon |
| `MANUAL_UNACKNOWLEDGED` / `UNKNOWN_ACK` | assumed or misspelled manual gates |
| `SYNTHETIC_FIXTURE` | the shipped fixtures, unless `--self-test` is passed |

Exit codes are `0` GO, `1` NO_GO, `2` a missing log, `3` a synthetic log set;
`GO` prints `NEXT=` and `HARDWARE_VERIFIED=0`, and every verdict line carries the
same flag.

Evidence: `tests/test_donor_gate.py` (15 tests: the GO path over the shipped
fixtures, the actuation-stage path, an unacknowledged gate, a misspelled gate, a
failing read-only gate, a card that moved, a stage that names no PCI id, two
cards in one stage, actuation without its predecessors, the synthetic refusal,
both usage errors, and that a GO never prints `HARDWARE_VERIFIED=1`). The
session document renders the gate from `docs/hardware_session.json`, so the plan
and the checker cannot drift, and `tests/test_hardware_session.py` still pins the
rendered file byte for byte.

What this does not do: it does not create hardware-in-the-loop. Nothing here
runs a machine, waits for a boot, or reads a log automatically; the operator
still supplies every file and every acknowledgement, and a GO repeats evidence
rather than producing it. `D5` therefore stays partial and `HARDWARE_VERIFIED`
stays 0.

### 11.20 B3/B4/B5/B8 — the admission policy is now tested, not just present

`GuCheckConfigPolicy` (139 lines, `src/checks.c`) is the only thing that decides
whether a discovered display function is admitted. Before this entry it had no
test of its own: the discovery suites link a hand-written
`GuCheckConfig` mock (`tests/gpu_discovery_mock.h`), which proves the callers
honour the answer but says nothing about the answer itself. Every refusal it
implements was therefore a promise, not a gate with a witness.

`tests/test_admission_gates.py` extracts `ConfigByte`, `ConfigWord`,
`GuCheckConfigPolicy`, `GuCheckConfig` and `GuCheckConfigInitialMaster` from the
real source, links them against independent host mocks, and runs 53 assertions
over crafted 256-byte config snapshots. The UEFI constants the policy depends on
(`PCI_CLASS_DISPLAY`, the command/status bits, the capability ids,
`PCI_EXPRESS_CAPABILITY_ID`, `PCI_POWER_STATE_D0`) are re-read from
`src/vendor/edk2/Include/IndustryStandard/Pci22.h`, `Pci23.h` and
`PciExpress21.h` and compared with the harness, so the test cannot drift away
from the firmware's own values. The capability-walk limits are extracted from
`checks.c` itself rather than retyped.

| Gate | Asserted refusals |
| --- | --- |
| Identity | unsupported vendor/device, class other than `0x03`, header type 1 (bridge); the multifunction bit is masked, not rejected |
| Decode | memory decode off, expansion ROM enable bit set, capability-list status bit clear |
| B3 | PMC version 0 or >3, PMCSR state D1/D2/D3, MSI enable set, MSI-X enable set, duplicate MSI capability |
| B4 | any capability id outside PM/MSI/MSI-X/PCIe/vendor; a vendor capability shorter than its 3-byte header |
| B5 | PCIe version 0 or 3, device type 2 (root complex); FLR bit 28 clear in Device Capabilities; Initiate FLR already set in Device Control; PM or PCIe capability missing |
| B8 | Bus Master set is refused by `GuCheckConfig` and accepted only by `GuCheckConfigInitialMaster` |
| Structure | `Out == NULL`, `Config == NULL`, segment/bus/device/function out of range, unaligned or sub-0x40 capability pointer, pointer past `0xfc`, self-looping chain, overlapping capabilities, a capability that runs past 256 bytes |

Two behaviours the harness pinned that the inventory text had wrong: only
PMCSR bits 1:0 are the power state (a set reserved bit 2 is still D0 and is
admitted), and the PCIe walk accepts device type 1 (legacy endpoint) while
refusing type 2 and above - so B5's old wording "link-status bit clear"
described nothing the code does. Both are corrected in the table above.

What this does not do: it does not admit a card. The harness's
`GuIsSupportedPciId` is a one-id stub (the real table is pinned separately by
`tests/test_gpu_device_ids.c`), the snapshots are synthetic, and nothing here
observes a real function's MSI/PM/PCIe registers. B1, B2 and B10 are untouched:
they need topology and memory-footprint evidence this pass does not produce.
The two `EFI_UNSUPPORTED` outcomes that this test makes predictable are still
`HARDWARE_VERIFIED=0`.

### 11.1 A1 — runtime target selection

| What | Where |
| --- | --- |
| New module: text parser, canonical formatter, variable read/write/delete | `src/gpu_selection.h`, `src/gpu_selection.c` |
| Variable name/GUID (fork-owned) | `GuTargets`, `5c1f2b40-8e21-4ef7-9d2b-7a113c5e8402` |
| Build switch; no `gpu-selection.h` is generated or read | `-RuntimeSelection` in both builders, `/DGU_RUNTIME_SELECTION` |
| Boot-time resolution, `ALL` policy, single-card default | `gpu_discovery.c` `ResolveRuntimeSelection`, `SelectPreparedRecords` |
| Console policy acquisition (auto single, numbered menu, `A`, `S`) | `app.c` `ResolveTargetsOnConsole` |
| Simulator models the variable | `sim/sim_world.c` `SimWorldSetTargets` |

Bounds: 128 targets, 4096-byte text, ASCII, `SSSS:BB:DD.F`, duplicates and
malformed forms refused with no partial list. A `GetVariable` that reports
`EFI_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL` is refused (`EFI_BAD_BUFFER_SIZE`), never truncated.

Evidence: sim scenarios `runtime-target` (binds `0000:01:00.0` chosen from the
variable with **no compiled list in the image**) and `runtime-absent`
(`0000:03:00.0` requested, no card there → refused, unbound platform, no BAR0
write, no FLR). Host unit `tests/test_gpu_selection.c` (80 checks: parser
matrix, 128/129 boundary, round-trip, variable store, oversized and malformed
stored text). Contract `tests/test_runtime_selection_contract.py` (16 tests,
including "a stale three-address `gpu-selection.h` in the include path is
ignored by a runtime-selection build").

Not closed by this: the *policy* still has no per-card record of which card was
already unlocked last boot (A7), and nothing yet proves two real cards.

### 11.2 A3 — multi-target admission

* `port.h`: `GU_RUNTIME_SELECTION` requires the ordered execution mode and is
  rejected next to `GU_SYNTHETIC_COMPILE_ONLY`/`GU_ACTIVE_SEQUENCE_PREPARE_ONLY`.
* `gpu_discovery.c`: the static `GU_GPU_SELECTION_COUNT != 1` gate now belongs
  to the compiled-list branch only. With runtime selection the count is unknown
  at build time, so the **runtime** gate decides: `selected_count != 1` without
  `GU_ACTUATION_ADMITTED` still refuses.
* No new admission path was added: the single switch
  (`GU_ACTUATION_ADMITTED`) and the waiver are untouched, and the synthetic
  profile is still structurally impossible to ship.

### 11.3 B6 — the BAR0 window is read, not assumed

`ReadBarWindow` (`gpu_discovery.c`) validates the firmware ACPI descriptor:
`Desc == 0x8a`, `Len == 43`, zero resource type and translation offset,
power-of-two `AddrLen >= 16 MiB`, base aligned to `AddrLen`, no
`AddrRangeMin + AddrLen` overflow, `AddrRangeMax == Min + Len - 1`. It releases
the descriptor through `FreePool` and refuses if the release cannot be proven
harmful — the release result is logged, never treated as a hardware fault.

`Gu.bar_size`/`bar_base` (from the descriptor, base cross-checked against a
64-bit decode of config `0x10`/`0x14`) are now authoritative in `profile.c`,
`msi_release.c`, `unlock_execution.c` and the S3 gate; the 16 MiB literal is
gone. A config/attribute disagreement is refused, so the change makes discovery
**stricter**, not looser.

Evidence: sim scenarios `rebar` (256 MiB window) and `bar-above-4g` (BAR0 at
`0x1_0000_0000`), both previously refused, now pass discovery and the full
transaction with the image reporting the assigned base/size.

### 11.4 B7 — device DMA under 4 GiB by request, not by luck

`GuDmaAllocate` now calls `AllocateBuffer(AllocateMaxAddress, ...)` with the
32-bit ceiling. The ownership rules are unchanged: any buffer the firmware
writes is retained if the call fails, retained if `Map` fails, and released
only when both `Unmap` and `FreeBuffer` succeed. The mapped-address check
(`dma > 0xffffffff`, alignment, truncation, `bytes-1 > 0xffffffff - dma`)
remains as the last line of defence.

Evidence: sim scenario `dma-high` (the model forces the 32-bit allocator to hand
out `0x1_0000_0000`): the transaction stops before any register write, no WPR2
window opens, no FLR, no fault is recorded, and no buffer is counted as mapped.
`tests/test_platform_bind_lifetime.py` re-executes the real allocator against
11 independent EFI error modes.

Honesty limit: the simulator cannot model the exact `AllocateMaxAddress`
ceiling; it models "32-bit unless the scenario forces 2^32". The firmware
contract that matters (never DMA above 4 GiB) is enforced in code twice.

### 11.6 A2 — runtime Windows-ESP identification

| What | Where |
| --- | --- |
| Structural predicate, no pin | `GuWindowsEspPathCandidate` (`gpu_windows_path.c/.h`) |
| Marker probe that does not latch the boot-file error state | `EspCarriesWindowsManager` (`boot_io.c`) |
| Both ESP sites select the runtime rule | asset reader `ReadPinnedAssetFromConfiguredEsp`, `GuBootLoadWindows` |
| Pin becomes conditional; the pinned default is unchanged | `boot_profile.h` (`GU_RUNTIME_ESP` branch, explicit comment) |
| Build switch | `-RuntimeEsp` → `/DGU_RUNTIME_ESP` in both builders |

The pinned path still demands `local/boot_profile.h` and an exact GUID match;
`GU_RUNTIME_ESP` + `GU_HOST_TEST_PROFILE` is a compile error, so a
synthetic-GUID image cannot be passed off as a runtime-ESP image.

Evidence: `tests/test_gpu_windows_path.c` (32 checks, now including 11 candidate
predicate cases), `tests/test_runtime_esp_contract.py` (12 tests: the pin is
still mandatory by default, the runtime branch carries no pin, both ESP sites
select it, the marker probe never latches `BootFileStatus`, the single-match
refusals survive, and the builders expose the switch). The UEFI sources compile
under `-DGU_RUNTIME_ESP` (checked by building the simulator with the define).

Coverage limit, stated plainly: the simulator does **not** exercise the runtime
ESP policy, because it models the asset volume and the Windows volume as two
directories, so no single modelled volume carries both. The runtime rule is
predicate-tested and compile-checked, not end-to-end tested, and has not been
run on hardware.

### 11.8 A7 — a record that survives a failed boot

| What | Where |
| --- | --- |
| Fixed-size validated record, two phases | `src/boot_state.h`, `src/boot_state.c` |
| Variable `GuBootState`, fork GUID `2a7d54c1-5b3e-4a19-8f60-9d21c4b7e803`, NV+BS+RT | `boot_state.c` |
| Reported once per boot for every entrypoint | `boot_io.c` (`GuBootOpen`) |
| Intent before the first mutation, outcome after the sequence | `app.c`, `dxe_main.c` |
| Reset path | `GuBootStateDelete` (delete the variable) |

Validation: exact size, magic, known phase, PCI field ranges, zero reserved
bytes. A short, long, or corrupt record is `EFI_COMPROMISED_DATA`, logged as
`BOOT_STATE PRESENT=0 READ_STATUS=... IGNORED=1`, and never repaired during
boot. Write failures are cast to void at both call sites, so a record problem
can never change a transaction's result.

Evidence: `tests/test_boot_state.c` (41 checks: validation matrix, phase
transitions, count advances only on outcome, write failure is inert, delete),
`tests/test_boot_state_contract.py` (10 tests: no control transfer depends on
the record, intent precedes the sequence, one read covers every entrypoint), and
the simulator runs all 9 scenarios with the record linked and reported.

What this does *not* do: it does not skip a card that was already processed, it
does not roll anything back, and it does not make re-application safe. Those
need the C1–C4 evidence.

### 11.9 A5 — one chip's offsets are not every chip's offsets

| What | Where |
| --- | --- |
| Captured-geometry table, one row per admitted Ada id | `src/gpu_sku_geometry.c` |
| `Refuses()` — the only predicate the gates use | `gpu_sku_geometry.h` |
| Refused at prepare, before any BAR access | `profile.c`, `GuAd104Prepare` |
| Refused in the vendor core before the one-shot attempt is consumed | `unlock_610.c`, `gpu_unlock_610_unlock` |
| AD102-only branches require a captured table | `unlock_610.c`, `is_ad102` |

The table classifies all 11 Ada ids the image admits. Only the reference AD102
pair (`0x2684`, `0x2685`) is marked captured; every AD103/104/106/107 id is
refused, and the device is not driven with offsets taken from another chip. The
refusal is reported as
`SKU_GEOMETRY=REFUSED DEVICE=2786 CHIP=AD104 SKU=RTX 4070 REASON=NO_CAPTURED_REGISTER_TABLE DIAGNOSTIC_ALLOWED=1`,
returns `EFI_UNSUPPORTED`, and leaves the platform untouched
(`PROFILE_VERIFIED=0 PROM_VERIFIED=0`, zero BAR writes, zero FLR, WPR2 unopened).
The read-only diagnostic does not consult the table: it is the mechanism by which
the missing capture is obtained.

Evidence: `tests/test_sku_geometry.c` (330 checks: table covers exactly
`GU_ADA_DEVICE_IDS`, complements hold, non-Ada ids are not answered by the gate,
no duplicate rows), `tests/test_sku_geometry_contract.py` (21 tests: refusal
precedes every hardware read and the state check, the vendor path refuses before
consuming the attempt, the diagnostic stays open, build wiring), the simulator
scenario `prepare ad104-sku` (`SIM_VERIFY=PASS SCENARIOS=10`), and host case 13 in
`tests/test_gpu_asset_lifetime.py` (the refusal costs zero reads).

Turing is refused twice over, which is the second half of the A5 exit
criterion:

| Where | What it refuses |
| --- | --- |
| `src/turing_assets.h` (compile time) | a build defining `GU_TURING_ACTUATION` — there is no payload to stage or hash, so such an image cannot exist |
| `src/turing_assets.h` (compile time) | a Turing manifest whose row count drifts from the reviewed five, so trimming the table cannot leave Turing cards admitted |
| `profile.c`, `RegistersFor` | a Turing card whose cold state does not match the passive predicate (`TURING_COLD=REFUSED`, `ACTIVE_ALLOWED=0`) |
| `profile.c`, `GuAd104Prepare` | the actuation path for any Turing card |

Evidence: `tests/test_turing_build_gate.py` (5 tests that compile a translation
unit including the header and require the compiler to fail with the explanation,
require it to succeed without the flag, and require a trimmed manifest to fail —
the tripwire is demonstrated, not asserted from source text).

What this does *not* do: it does not make any captured table a verified
transaction. `ACTUATION_VERIFIED=0` still holds for the reference AD102, and the
AD104/106/107 rows stay empty until a dump exists. Ampere keeps its documented
generic path, unchanged by this gate. And the build gate says nothing about
whether the pinned Turing hashes are right — only that a Turing actuation image
cannot be produced from this tree.

### 11.10 A6 — the bundle can be staged once, and says so

| What | Where |
| --- | --- |
| Fixed-size validated record, `GuAssetInstall` variable | `src/asset_install.[ch]` |
| Bundle digest over names, sizes and pinned hashes | `GuAssetInstallBundleDigest` |
| `ABSENT`/`CURRENT`/`STALE`/`CORRUPT` decision | `GuAssetInstallState` |
| Staging build: verify → copy → read back → record | `boot_io.c`, `GuAssetInstallStage` |
| Entrypoint, never reaches prepare or the sequence | `app.c` (`GU_ASSET_INSTALL_ONLY`) |
| Report at open and at load | `boot_io.c` (`ASSET_INSTALL PRESENT=…`, `STATE=…`) |

Every file is verified against its pinned SHA-256 before it is written, written
in ≤1 MiB pieces, flushed, closed, and then read back and hashed again; the
record is written only after all five succeed. An existing file is accepted only
when it already holds the pinned bytes — a mismatch is refused
(`REASON=… EXISTING_MISMATCH=1`), never overwritten, so an interrupted install is
resumable and a foreign file is not silently replaced. The installer refuses
when the image was not launched from removable media, or when any GPU state is
non-idle, and it touches no BAR: zero writes, zero FLRs.

Evidence: `tests/test_asset_install.c` (112 checks: digest determinism and
sensitivity, validation matrix, CURRENT/STALE/CORRUPT, NVRAM round trip, refused
write is inert), `tests/test_asset_install_contract.py` (24 tests: the launch
rule is not relaxed, only the install build stages, every file is verified twice,
no overwrite and no delete, the record is the commit point, the pinned version is
singular), the simulator scenario `prepare install-assets` (stages 5 files,
reports `CURRENT`, repeated install is idempotent, zero BAR writes), and
`tests/test_gpu_asset_lifetime.py` (host load path over the staged report).

What this does *not* do: it does not make the ESP a place the image may be
launched from (that guard is the only thing preventing unattended re-application,
whose safety is unproven), and it does not authenticate the vendor signature — a
digest proves these bytes, not who signed them. Both remain C3/C4/D1.

### 11.11 A4 — a card the image was not built for is refused

The compile-time profile is still compile-time. What changed is that the choice
is now a *precondition* rather than a comment: `GU_STOCK_PROFILE_SS0` was a
constant the image carried and never compared against anything, so a build for
one card would run its destructive path on another card presenting a different
cold value.

| Piece | Where | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Predicate | `src/stock_profile.h` | `GuStockProfileAccepts(Observed, HasExpected, Expected)` — a build with no expectation accepts, a build with one compares |
| Gate | `src/profile.c`, `RegistersFor` | after the selector sanity rules, before anything else; sets `StockProfileMismatch` and logs, never faults |
| Refusal | `GuAd104Prepare` | returns `EFI_UNSUPPORTED` with the card untouched |
| Message | log | `STOCK_PROFILE=REFUSED COMPILED=… EXPECTED_SS0=… OBSERVED_SS0=… REASON=CARD_DOES_NOT_MATCH_BUILD`; a match logs `STOCK_PROFILE=MATCH` |
| Linkability | `src/port.c`, `src/port.h` | the entry-latch API is declared for every profile, with an explicit no-op branch for the policies that keep no latch |
| Selector step | `src/vendor/unlock_610.c` | the four-phase selector machine runs only in `_FULL`; every other policy refuses the step instead of writing selectors the port layer would fault on |

That last row is a finding, not a nicety: before this pass three of the four
profiles **did not link**. The latch API and the selector phase were
unconditional call sites with `#ifdef`-guarded definitions, so
`entryLatchedSs1Preserve`, `original03100062` and `observed03000062` compiled and
then failed at link time — the "one image, four profiles" matrix was really one
image, and nothing in CI ever built the other three.

Linking them exposed a second half of the same defect: the *transaction* existed
only in the full policy. The other three linked and then refused the selector
step, so they could not perform an unlock at all. Each policy now has its own
selector contract, and the checks that follow the write compare against that
contract instead of a constant:

| Profile | Selectors | Follow-up checks | Log |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `entryLatchedSs1Full` | SS0, then one SS1 write, authorised by the phase machine | SS1 must be `0x8`, phase must be `TARGET` | `SELECTOR_PATH=PHASED` |
| `entryLatchedSs1Preserve` | SS0 only; SS1 is refused by the port layer and left as found | SS1 must equal the latched entry value | `SELECTOR_PATH=PRESERVE` |
| `original03100062`, `observed03000062` | both, in stock order, no phase | SS1 must be `0x8`; no phase to check | `SELECTOR_PATH=UNTRACKED` |

Three call sites had to become policy-aware for that to be true: the pre-FLR
comparison, the post-FLR comparison, and the pre-close silicon check in
`msi_release.c` — each expected `SS1==0x8`, so a preserve build faulted after its
own reset. The non-latched policies still have no protection against a repeated
SS1 write; that guard is full-policy only, and the build says so rather than
implying otherwise.

Evidence: `tests/test_stock_profile.c` (12 checks, gcc and clang under UBSan:
mismatch refuses, match accepts, no expectation accepts, no fault, message
fields), `tests/test_stock_profile_contract.py` (14 tests: placement after the
sanity rules, read-only, `EFI_UNSUPPORTED`, message fields, profile table, no
runtime NVRAM selector), `tests/test_stock_profile_matrix.py` (8 tests: the
matrix builds and links every profile, and each policy keeps its own selector
contract), and four simulator rows — `prepare stock-match` and `prepare
stock-mismatch` differ only in the card (the mismatch row reports
`STATUS=8000000000000003 BAR_WRITES=0 FLR=0` and names the build), and
`transaction preserve` / `transaction untracked` run a full transaction under
those policies: preserve reports `SEL_WRITES=1:0` (one SS0 write, no SS1 write)
and still completes, untracked reports `SEL_WRITES=1:1` in stock order.

What this does *not* do: it does not choose a profile at runtime. The two
