entry-latched policies are indistinguishable before the write — that is what
"entry-latched" means — so no probe can pick between them, and the expectations
for the non-latched policies do not exist in this repository. Operator selection
with the choice recorded in the A7 record (§11.8) is still open.

### 11.12 A8 — the firmware timer can now be bounded

`GuBootOpen` used to disable the firmware timer and never re-arm it, so a hang
inside the sequence left the machine frozen with a half-written card. The timer
is now programmed in exactly one place and cancelled at one place:

| Piece | Where | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Threshold | `GU_WATCHDOG_SECONDS` | build constant, default `0` = arms nothing, disables the timer exactly as before |
| Arm | `WatchdogProgram`, called from `GuBootOpen` | `seconds × 10,000,000` in the firmware's 100 ns unit, reset code `0` |
| Sanity | `GU_WATCHDOG_MAX_SECONDS` (3600) | a longer value is refused with `REASON=IMPLAUSIBLE_THRESHOLD` rather than armed |
| Cancel | `GuBootWatchdogCancel`, called from `app.c` | after the outcome is recorded, before `GuBootWindows`; logs `WATCHDOG=CANCELLED SECONDS=…` |
| Record | log | `WATCHDOG BOUND=… ACTIVE=1` or `REASON=NO_BUILD_THRESHOLD`, before the first mutation |

The default build is unchanged on purpose: no worst-case duration has been
measured, and a timer shorter than the transaction resets a machine mid-write,
which is worse than the hang it replaces. A prepare-only build returns before the
arm site, so it still touches neither the timer nor any boot state.

Evidence: `tests/test_watchdog_contract.py` (10 tests: two programming sites,
arm inside `GuBootOpen` after the prepare-only return, sanity check before
programming, 100 ns conversion, report helper is read-only, cancel reports and
clears, cancel after the outcome and before Windows, log states whether a bound
was in force), and the simulator row `transaction watchdog`, which builds with
`GU_WATCHDOG_SECONDS=600` and reports `SIM_WATCHDOG ARMS=1 BOUND=600
CANCELLED=1` after a transaction that still completed. The default build is
pinned too: the other transaction rows assert that nothing was armed.

What this does *not* do: it does not choose a threshold. That needs the measured
budgets from C2/C6, and it does not attempt recovery — the timer's only job is to
turn a hang into a reboot that the A7 record then explains.

### 11.13 Multi-GPU step 2 — per-card firmware acceptance

The structural PROM check answers a weak question: is this 1 MiB readout a valid
VBIOS naming this PCI device. Any card of the right family can present one, and
the log has always said `SIGNATURE_AUTHENTICATED=0`. Step 2 of the multi-GPU plan
asks for an authenticated per-device reference instead, which is the part that can
be settled without hardware.

| Piece | Where | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Allowlist | `src/prom_reference.c` | static const table of (device id, subsystem id, ROM SHA-256, loader version); **empty in the shipped image** |
| Decision | `GuPromReferenceDecide` | exact hit on all four, or one of `UNKNOWN_CARD`, `DIGEST_MISMATCH`, `LOADER_MISMATCH`, `MALFORMED` |
| Requirement | `GU_PROM_REFERENCE_REQUIRED` | a miss becomes a refusal; a build without it keeps the structural check and says so |
| Preparation | `profile.c`, `GuAd104Prepare` | passes `TRUE`: with the requirement, a miss is `EFI_UNSUPPORTED` and nothing is written |
| Transaction | `unlock_610.c`, FWSEC step | passes `TRUE` as well: the same requirement before the first write |
| Diagnostic | `profile.c`, `GuDiagnosticScan` | passes `FALSE`: it reports the digest, device and subsystem, which is how a reference is captured in the first place |
| Message | log | `PROM_IDENTITY=VERIFIED …` or `PROM_IDENTITY=REFUSED DEVICE=… SUBSYS=… SHA256=… REASON=… REFS=… DIAGNOSTIC_ALLOWED=1` |

**No reference is committed, and that is the finding.** This repository contains
no card dumps, so the allowlist is empty and a build with the requirement admits
nothing. That is the fail-closed default doing its job rather than a defect: a
digest invented to make the admitted path look green would be worse than no
reference at all, because it would assert provenance nobody observed.

The one entry that exists is synthetic and cannot ship: `GU_PROM_REFERENCE_SYNTHETIC`
pins the *simulator's* model ROM, is rejected with `#error` in any unhosted build
or next to `GU_SIMULATED_ACTUATION`, and names itself in its `Origin` field. It
exists so the admitted path is executed rather than merely compiled.

What this does not do: it does not authenticate a signature. Both decision paths
keep `SIGNATURE_AUTHENTICATED=0`, and the Windows 617.42 Booter provenance
comparison is still mandatory evidence that nothing here provides. It also does
not replace the per-target admission gates; it narrows what counts as "the right
card" inside them.

Evidence: `tests/test_prom_reference.c` (two builds of the same module: the
synthetic table accepts the exact tuple and refuses wrong device, wrong subsystem,
wrong digest, wrong loader, short/long/uppercase/non-hex digests; the shipped
table admits nothing including the synthetic identity), `tests/test_prom_reference_contract.py`
(17 tests: no runtime registration, empty table, exact matching, requirement is
compile-time and applied at preparation and in the transaction but not in the
diagnostic, `EFI_UNSUPPORTED` mapping, message fields, no authentication claim,
synthetic cannot reach firmware, one version literal), and two simulator rows:
`prepare prom-refused` (`STATUS=8000000000000003 BAR_WRITES=0 FLR=0`,
`REASON=UNKNOWN_CARD REFS=0`) and `prepare prom-admitted`
(`PROM_IDENTITY=VERIFIED`).

### 11.14 S1/D2 — the admitted image is built and diffed

S1's exit criteria end with "CI builds and diffs the admitted image", and D2 asks
for a CI build of the waiver path. Neither had a mechanism: the workflow built
preparation-only images, and `GU_ACTIVE_UNVERIFIED_ACTUATION` - the single switch
that turns "refuses to actuate" into "may attempt the unverified transaction" -
was described only in a runbook.

`tools/waiver_build_diff.py` builds every source in the image twice from the same
tree and diffs each translation unit:

| Compared | Expected |
| --- | --- |
| Preprocessor defines | exactly two deltas: `GU_ACTIVE_UNVERIFIED_ACTUATION` appears, `GU_ACTUATION_ADMITTED` flips `0 -> 1`; anything else is an unreviewed change and fails |
| Defined object symbols | none, in either direction: the waiver flips a gate inside the same program, it does not compile a different one |
| Reach | `GU_ACTUATION_ADMITTED` must flip in at least one unit, so a waiver that admits nothing cannot pass as evidence |

Current result: `WAIVER_DIFF=PASS SOURCES=26 MACRO_DELTAS=41 ADMITTED_UNITS=15
SYMBOL_DELTAS=0`. The 41 deltas are the flag reaching all 26 units plus the
admission constant in the 15 that include `port.h`.

What this does not do: it is a hosted GCC build of the same sources with the
simulator's define shim, so it witnesses source shape, not that MSVC/EDK II emit
the same image. It also does not build with a synthetic GUID, the second half of
D2 - that is a build-script change in `src/Build-Experimental-MSVC.ps1`, which
cannot be executed here and is left open rather than claimed.

**The second half - the same image, built by MSVC.** The diff is evidence about
source shape under GCC. The Windows job now compiles the admitted image for real:
application and DXE, one target and an ordered two-target sequence, each asserting
the exact binary its selection label implies. The admitted build passes
`-RuntimeEsp`, because the pinned path needs the private, gitignored
`local/boot_profile.h`, a hosted runner has no reviewed GUID, and a waived build
may not use the synthetic host-test GUID. Nothing is uploaded: the artifact globs
cannot match an admitted name, and `tests/test_waiver_ci.py` fails if one ever
could. The waiver's interlocks are asserted to still refuse before any compiler
runs.

Making the Windows and host jobs actually execute this branch's code found three
defects the host suite had been hiding - each is now covered:

* `src/prom_reference.c` was compiled into no MSVC image, so every variant failed
  to link its own `profile.c` calls. `tests/test_build_source_lists.py` now pins
  each builder's source list to the program the simulator compiles, and checks
  that every `Gu*` symbol a unit imports is defined by some listed unit;
* `test_boot_binding_contract.py` held two pins that only run where clang exists,
  so they had never executed locally: an ordering assertion made inside a slice
  that cannot contain the thing it looked for, and open-site counts pinned to 9
  where the staged bundle had added sites. The ordering is now compared over the
  whole source and the counts are replaced by the property (every open result is
  handled);
* the discovery mock scanned `&gpu[i].bar` to 4096 over a 24-entry array, so which
  compiler's static layout put the pool buffer there decided whether the free was
  counted. Bounded by the array size.

Evidence: the tool itself (CI runs it), `tests/test_waiver_build_diff.py` (10
tests: the diff passes, a missing compiler is a skip rather than a pass, the pin
is exactly the reviewed pair, no unit may gain or lose code, the profile matches
the runbook, every compiled source is covered, no dependency on generated state),
`tests/test_waiver_ci.py` (10 tests), `tests/test_build_source_lists.py` (4 tests).
Workflow run 44445509664 and later on this branch: `host=success efi=success`.

### 11.16 S3/C1 — a pre-Stop capture, and the contract it feeds

Step 3 of `MULTI_GPU_REFACTOR_REVIEW.md` §4.3 asks for "a documented bound and a
pre-Stop state capture for the AD102/GA102 Stop callback, then a per-target
contract that requires ...". The capture and the contract exist now; the bound
does not, and nothing is admitted that was not admitted before.

`src/stop_contract.[ch]` is a pure decision over an explicit observation: ten
requirements, each a bit, and `ALLOW` only when every one holds. A zero-initialised
observation (or a NULL one) satisfies nothing, so the fail-closed direction is a
property of the type rather than of the caller. `GuStopContractDescribe` spells the
missing set out, and the requirement order is the plan's order.

`GuMsiRelease` logs one `STOP_CONTRACT` line, twice over:

| Site | What it can claim | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Immediately before the wholesale refusal | `OWNER` only | the refusal deliberately precedes every other check (`test_release_handoff_contract.py` pins that ordering) |
| Immediately before each `Driver()` call | `OWNER`, `COLD`, `CONSOLE`, `PEERS` | those four just returned success in the same iteration |
| Always | the other six are `0` | no code in this tree observes the target's firmware GOP, a closed intent log, an executed recovery, the 617.42 Booter comparison, a Stop bound, or DMA idleness |

The six unobservable facts are fields in the record, not omissions: the line names
them in `MISSING`, so a hardware run knows exactly what it has to establish. A
capture that guessed would be worse than one that says so.

Evidence: `tests/test_stop_contract.c` (72 checks under ASan+UBSan: zero
observation refuses, each requirement is independently necessary, the description
is ordered and bounded, the shipped capture is incomplete by construction);
`tests/test_stop_contract_contract.py` (12 source checks: capture before callback,
before refusal, never claims an unobservable fact, one implementation of the
decision, requirement order equals the plan). CI compiles and runs both.

What it is not: the refusal is unchanged, `DECISION` is `REFUSE` on every capture
this image can produce, and no line says a Stop is safe. The bound and the recovery
evidence are still steps 3-5 of the plan, and they need hardware.

### 11.17 B9 — the image can now start from the ESP, and only when it can prove it

B9 said "launched from USB with a writable log directory", which meant a machine
could never run this from its own disk. The rule is now a decision
(`src/launch_source.[ch]`) over seven observations, and it has two ways to say
yes:

| Launch | Decision | Requires |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Removable media | `ALLOW_REMOVABLE` | nothing further; the stick is the path everything was written for |
| The Windows ESP | `ALLOW_RESIDENT` | partition volume **and** a `GU_ESP_RESIDENT` build **and** a Windows loader on it **and** the pin matched **and** the bundle record present **and** the log directory writable |
| Anything else | `REFUSE` | — the line names the first gate that failed |

The refusal is the interesting half. Every non-USB launch in every other build now
logs `LAUNCH_SOURCE DECISION=REFUSE REASON=BUILD_REFUSES_ESP_RESIDENT …` and returns
`EFI_ACCESS_DENIED` — the same behaviour as before, but it says why instead of
looking like a broken device path. In a resident build the same decision is
re-evaluated after the log file is created, because `LOG_WRITABLE` is only
provable there; there is deliberately no single pre-open decision that would have
to guess.

Three interlocks keep this from becoming a second, quieter admission path:

* `GU_ESP_RESIDENT` without `GU_RUNTIME_ESP` is a compile error, and both builders
  throw on `-EspResident` without `-RuntimeEsp`; a pinned build would tie the
  image to one machine, which is the coupling A2 removed.
* `-EspResident` with `-SyntheticCompileProfile` is refused by both builders, so
  the simulator's synthetic build can never claim the relaxation.
* Installation is untouched: `GuAssetInstallStage` still refuses a non-removable
  volume (`ASSET_INSTALL REASON=IMAGE_NOT_ON_REMOVABLE_MEDIA`). A resident image
  runs from the ESP but must still be *installed* from the stick, and the
  admission line says so (`INSTALL_STILL_REQUIRES_USB=1
  ACTUATION_GATES_UNCHANGED=1`).

Evidence: `tests/test_launch_source.c` (126 checks under ASan+UBSan: all 64
observation masks decide and name a reason without ever disagreeing, removable is
unconditional, each gate is independently necessary);
`tests/test_launch_source_contract.py` (12 source checks: default build refuses and
logs the reason, the compile interlock, both builder interlocks, the install gate
still refuses, `BootFromUsb` is set only inside the removable branch, one
definition and one declaration of the ESP probe, every reason is named). CI
compiles the C test with gcc and clang and runs the source checks.

What it is not: nothing here has been booted from an ESP. No donor machine has run
a resident build, `LAUNCH_SOURCE=ESP_RESIDENT_WINDOWS_ESP` has never appeared in a
real log, and the simulator cannot produce it (its image is not a UEFI volume). B9
stays partial until a donor run shows that line and the six `MISSING` facts from
the Stop contract on the same boot.

### 11.18 S5 / D-class — the donor session as gates, not a checklist

The donor card and the programmer are on the bench, so the first hardware run is
now defined as three stages with a mechanical check after each:
`docs/hardware_session.json` is the source of truth, `docs/DONOR_HARDWARE_SESSION.md`
is rendered from it, and `tools/verify_run_log.py` scores a captured log against
the same manifest.

| Stage | What it may do | The gate that ends it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `readonly` | enumerate, print eligibility as false | `R2_ENUMERATION_COMPLETED`: the scan reached its count line, with `CAN_DETACH=0 CAN_UNLOCK=0` in the log |
| `prepare` | run the preflight, refuse before any mutation | `P1_...`: the entrypoint prints `BEFORE_MUTATION=1` and no step, waiver or Stop line appears |
| `actuate` | one ordered card, waiver recorded once | `A5_...`: a *later* boot reads the record the run left, with `TOO_FEW_LOGS` when the operator supplies only one |

Two design choices make it hard to fool:

* **The tokens are format strings.** A gate requires the printf format string
  that emits the line, converted to a pattern at check time, so a gate cannot be
  satisfied by text no build of this tree writes. `tests/test_hardware_session.py`
  asserts every token is present in the file the manifest names and that none is
  mostly wildcards.
* **The verdict is bounded.** `HARDWARE_VERIFIED=0` is printed on every run; the
  nine `NOT_PROVEN` facts (617.42 Booter, target GOP, closed log, executed
  recovery, Stop bound, DMA idleness, Windows device start, CUDA throughput,
  cold state after power loss) are printed on every run, pass or fail; a log
  carrying the fixture marker is refused outright unless `--self-test` is given,
  and a self-test verdict can never read `PASS`.

The six `MANUAL` gates are the ones no script can check and the ones that matter
most on a donor: the programmer and known-good image on the bench, the card's
serial recorded, the log medium empty, exactly one NVIDIA card, a `HALTED` step
ending the session rather than the loop, and Windows started with the card
enumerated afterwards. They are printed on every run so that they are skipped
only deliberately.

The bench has its own half: `tools/session_preflight.py` refuses a medium that
already carries a `RUNnnnn.TXT` (a stale file is indistinguishable from a live
one), a `local/boot_profile.h` that still holds the committed placeholder GUID,
and an image that is empty or not a PE, while recording the image's SHA256 for
the session log.

Evidence: `tests/test_hardware_session.py` (42 tests: token grounding, stage
well-formedness, printf-to-pattern conversion, the verifier passing a good
read-only/prepare/actuation log and failing a truncated one, a simulated one, a
doubled waiver and a Stop in a preparation session, the synthetic refusal, the
rendered document being byte-identical to the manifest, the pre-flight failing a
stale medium and the placeholder GUID, and no output ever printing
`HARDWARE_VERIFIED=1`). CI runs the renderer, two scored fixtures and the suite.

What it is not: no gate has been evaluated against a real log, because no donor
run has happened. The fixtures are hand-written models of what such a log would
contain, marked `SYNTHETIC_FIXTURE_NOT_A_HARDWARE_RUN` so they can never be
mistaken for a capture. The gates say what a run must do; they do not say a card
will survive it, and the readiness tracker still counts hardware evidence as
0 of 43.

### 11.19 D1 — the images are signed, and the signing says what it proves

D1 listed "artifacts are unsigned; Secure Boot must be off or a certificate
enrolled by hand". The second half is now a script instead of a manual step, and
the first half is answered only for one machine.

`docs/image_variants.json` is every image this repository can build - 31 variants
across the four builders (three runtime-selection preparation images are recorded
as not buildable, with the source rule that refuses them) - as data. `src/Build-Sign-Deploy-UniversalGPU.ps1`
executes that catalogue: build, prove the reported flags, sign inside WSL with a
personal certificate, verify, receipt. `docs/BUILD_SIGN_DEPLOY.md` is the user
document and its matrix table is rendered from the same file.

Three properties make it hard to misuse:

* **The signature is checked against the firmware, not against itself.** Before
  signing, the script reads `db` with `Get-SecureBootUEFI`, walks the
  `EFI_SIGNATURE_LIST` entries and refuses unless the DER certificate it is about
  to sign with is byte-identical to one already enrolled. A signature the
  firmware will not trust is a boot loop, not a security property, and the script
  cannot produce one silently. `-SkipDbCheck` records `DB_ENROLLED=UNKNOWN`.
* **The private key never leaves WSL.** `sbsign` runs there, the key lives in the
  WSL user's home, and Windows only ever passes base64 blobs inside a
  base64-encoded bash payload - the same transport the reference helper needed
  because path-shaped arguments across the boundary corrupt backslashes.
* **Signing cannot promote an image.** Each variant carries a safety class
  (`read-only`, `refuses-before-mutation`, `compile-only`, `stop-only`,
  `actuates`) and the catalogue's expected output filename; the script fails when
  the builder's own `STATUS=` line disagrees with either. Only `-Only <id>
  -StageDrive <letter>` stages anything, `stop-only`/`actuates` additionally need
  `-AcceptActuatingDeploy`, and a DXE driver can never be staged because the
  firmware will not run a PE subsystem 11 image as `BOOTX64.EFI`.

Evidence: `tests/test_image_variants.py` (30 tests: every builder exists and links
the subsystem the catalogue claims, every switch is a parameter of that builder,
every output name is recomputed from the builders' own naming rules, every
attestation names a field the builder prints, the safety classes agree with the
switches, the dual Stop never appears without pinned handoff, the script refuses
matrix staging and DXE staging and checks `db`, its PowerShell is 5.1-compatible
and brace-balanced, and the rendered matrix is byte-identical to the catalogue).
CI runs the renderer and the suite on Linux, and parses the script with
`[Parser]::ParseFile` on `windows-latest` - parse only, never executed.

What it is not: a release signing story. There is no CA, no timestamp, no
reproducibility claim, and the certificate is personal to one machine. A signed
image is the image you built and the firmware will load it; nothing here says the
firmware accepts it, that the card survives it, or that Windows starts the
device. Every receipt carries `HardwareVerified: false` and
`Windows61742BooterProven: false`, and the closing status line carries
`HARDWARE_VERIFIED=0`.

### 11.15 S5/A8 — the recovery matrix, checked against the code

A8's exit criteria ask for a "documented, tested recovery matrix (mid-transaction
power loss, Stop hang, FLR refusal, partial multi-GPU) with a software-visible
state that survives the failure". The state exists (§11.8, §11.12); the matrix did
not, and prose written from memory is exactly what this repository keeps finding
to be wrong.

`docs/recovery_matrix.json` is the source of truth and
`docs/RECOVERY_MATRIX.md` is rendered from it, so the two cannot drift. Eight
classes, each with the same shape:

| Field | Must be |
| --- | --- |
| Symptom | a log line the named source file actually emits (the token is the format string) |
| Record | fields of `GU_BOOT_STATE`, the only state that outlives a failed boot |
| Record state | what those fields read in this class |
| Card / machine state | what the code leaves behind, and why |
| Steps | ordered, per card, no retries |
| Proof | what a later boot must show |
| Simulator | the row that exercises the software half, or `none` |
| Not verified | what nobody has demonstrated |

The four classes A8 names are all present (`power-loss-mid-transaction`,
`stop-hang`, `function-reset-refused`, `partial-multi-target`), plus
`dma-buffers-retained`, `wpr2-left-open`, `card-refused-before-any-write` and
`asset-install-incomplete`.

Evidence: `tests/test_recovery_matrix.py` (10 tests) fails if a symptom token is
absent from the file it names, if a cited record field is not a `GU_BOOT_STATE`
field, if a named simulator row does not exist, if a class disappears, if any
class claims `verified: true`, or if the rendered document is not byte-identical
to the manifest. `tools/render_recovery_matrix.py --write` regenerates the
document.

What this does not do: it does not demonstrate any recovery. Every class is marked
unverified with the reason, `RECOVERY_VERIFIED` stays false, and no procedure here
has been executed on hardware. It also cannot cover C6 (timeout policy) - a bound
is still unmeasured, which is why the watchdog stays opt-in (§11.12).

### 11.7 Items deliberately not changed

* **A4 (stock profile)** and **A5 (Turing payload, per-SKU tables)** need
  per-SKU cold-state evidence that this repository does not contain; A5 now
  refuses what it cannot drive (§11.9). Choosing a profile or
  emitting a Turing patch from the current constants would be a guess in the
  most destructive part of the path, so nothing was changed there.
* **A8 (watchdog)**: the arm/cancel mechanism exists but no threshold is
  chosen (§11.12). Nobody knows the worst-case duration, and arming a timer
  shorter than it would reset a machine mid-transaction, which is worse than the
  current hang. The default build still arms nothing until C2/C6 produce the
  bound.
* **A6/A7 (asset install, persisted state/rollback)**: the install step and the
  boot record now exist (§11.8, §11.10); what remains is the signature story
  (D1) and any behaviour that would skip or roll back a transaction.

### 11.5 Not touched by this pass

A2 (build-time ESP GUID), A5 (Turing payload), A6 (asset install/hash
pinning), A7 (persisted state/rollback), A8 (watchdog recovery), and every
class-C item that needs hardware remain exactly as inventoried above, except
where §11.11 and §11.12 record what did change.
